title: Crescent Wealth x Redwood — POC scoping (Private/VPC inference)
summary: Crescent Wealth scoped a 2–3 week technical evaluation focused on a regulated, advisor-facing workflow: summarization + retrieval over internal research/CRM notes and compliance-friendly drafting for client communications. Crescent wants Private/VPC deployment (or equivalent isolated environment) due to PII/financial data, with audit logs and KMS integration. The team discussed workload characteristics (burstiness, concurrency), model candidates (70B-class + smaller fallback), requirements for structured JSON output/tool calling, and acceptable fallback behaviors. Redwood proposed a milestone plan: Week 1 environment + connectivity + baseline perf, Week 2 application integration and caching/batching tuning, Week 3 security review artifacts + sizing/procurement readiness.
next_steps: Redwood (Colin) to send a one-pager POC plan + environment checklist (VPC connectivity, DNS/TLS, allowlists) by 2026-01-22
Crescent (Maya/Tom) to share 10–20 representative prompts (sanitized) + target output schemas (JSON) by 2026-01-23
Redwood (Fatima) to recommend 2–3 model options (primary + fallback) and expected latency/cost tradeoffs by 2026-01-24
Crescent (Elena) to send security questionnaire “lite” + required evidence list; Redwood to respond with approved FAQ language by 2026-01-27
Schedule a 90-min technical deep dive on routing/fallback and sizing (Crescent platform + Redwood SE) for week of 2026-01-27
action_items: Colin O'Donnell (Redwood) — Send POC milestones + Private/VPC connectivity checklist — Due 2026-01-22

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Crescent Wealth x Redwood — POC scoping (Private/VPC inference)
Date: 2026-01-21
Time: 3:00pm ET
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Hannah Schmitt, Colin O'Donnell, Fatima Noor
Crescent Wealth: Maya Patel, Tom Reynolds, Elena Garcia

---

[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. Okay, I think we’re all on. Thanks everybody for making time. This is our POC scoping call. Goal is we leave with a crisp plan for a two to three week eval, what “done” looks like, and who owns what.

[00:16] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[00:17] Tom Reynolds: Yep.

[00:18] Elena Garcia: Good.

[00:20] Hannah Schmitt: Quick intros. I’m Hannah, AE. Colin is solutions, does a lot of Private and VPC deployments. Fatima is our regulated SE, she’ll keep us honest on the security and compliance boundaries.

[00:33] Colin O'Donnell: Hey everyone.

[00:34] Fatima Noor: Hi.

[00:36] Hannah Schmitt: And Crescent folks—Maya, Tom, Elena—anything you want to add on roles?

[00:41] Maya Patel: Sure. I lead platform engineering. We own cloud networking, Kubernetes, identity, that kind of thing.

[00:48] Tom Reynolds: I run data and ML. My team is building the first few LLM use cases and the evaluation harness.

[00:54] Elena Garcia: I’m GRC and security. I’m the person who gets pulled into the “where does data go and how long do you keep it” conversations.

[01:02] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect. Tom, do you want to restate the target workload, just so we’re aligned?

[01:07] Tom Reynolds: Yeah. The first thing we actually want to productionize is an advisor workflow. Think—an “advisor copilot” inside our internal portal. It does two main things: one, pulls together a summary of a client situation from CRM notes and recent communications. Two, drafts suggested email language or call notes, but it has to be compliant—like we can’t hallucinate performance promises and we need citations to internal sources.

[01:33] Colin O'Donnell: When you say citations—do you mean like “source: document X / timestamp” style?

[01:37] Tom Reynolds: Exactly. We have internal research PDFs, meeting notes, sometimes recorded call transcripts. We’re building a retrieval layer. So prompt includes a set of snippets, and we want the model to produce structured JSON: summary, recommended next steps, and a citations array.

[01:55] Fatima Noor: And just to confirm, the data in those snippets includes PII and financial account context?

[02:00] Tom Reynolds: Yes. Definitely PII. Sometimes balances. Sometimes, uh, suitability type data.

[02:06] Elena Garcia: We treat it as regulated. It’s not HIPAA, but it’s still sensitive. Our policy is: no sending that to a public multi-tenant service without strict controls.

[02:17] Hannah Schmitt: Makes sense. So on deployment mode—my understanding from prior call is you’re leaning Private/VPC, not hosted shared API.

[02:26] Maya Patel: Correct. If there’s a way to do a short technical evaluation without standing up a full on-prem thing, great, but it has to be isolated. VPC is the baseline.

[02:37] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. For this pilot we can scope it as Private deployment in your VPC, with customer-managed networking. We’ll need to align on connectivity pattern—peering vs PrivateLink style, DNS, and egress.

[02:49] Maya Patel: We’re on AWS. Peering is okay. PrivateLink also possible but takes longer internally.

[02:57] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Peering is usually faster for a POC.

[03:00] Hannah Schmitt: Can we talk success criteria? Like, what would make you say “this works, we want to proceed”?

[03:06] Tom Reynolds: Three buckets. Quality: The citations must be correct, and the JSON formatting must be valid—our app can’t handle random prose. Performance: we have advisors waiting, so time-to-first-token and overall latency matter. And then security: audit logs, retention, and encryption.

[03:26] Hannah Schmitt: On performance, do you have targets? Even rough.

[03:29] Tom Reynolds: Rough. For a typical interaction maybe 1–2k input tokens including retrieved chunks, and output 300 to 800 tokens. We’d like first token in under a second, and full response under, say, 5 to 6 seconds. We can tolerate longer for “deep research” mode but the day-to-day summary needs to feel snappy.

[03:52] Colin O'Donnell: Concurrency / QPS expectations?

[03:54] Tom Reynolds: During peak, maybe 20 to 30 concurrent users. Not all generating at once. Maybe bursts of 5–10 requests per second during certain hours.

[04:06] Maya Patel: Our internal portal usage is spiky. Also we’ll eventually expand to client communications review—like scanning outbound emails for policy violations.

[04:17] Fatima Noor: That latter workload is more batchy, right? Like a queue.

[04:20] Maya Patel: Exactly.

[04:21] Hannah Schmitt: Okay, that’s helpful for sizing and also for batching/caching.

[04:26] Colin O'Donnell: On the JSON requirement—we can talk about structured outputs. Do you already have a schema?

[04:31] Tom Reynolds: We do. It’s something like:
- client_summary: string
- risks: array of {category, description}
- recommended_next_actions: array
- citations: array of {doc_id, snippet_id, confidence}
- compliance_flags: array

[04:48] Colin O'Donnell: Great. We’ll want a few examples. And we should decide if you want strict JSON mode (no trailing text) or if you can tolerate minor formatting errors.

[04:57] Tom Reynolds: Strict, please.

[04:58] Elena Garcia: Strict also helps from an audit perspective, honestly.

[05:03] Hannah Schmitt: Model preferences—what have you tried so far?

[05:06] Tom Reynolds: We tested Azure OpenAI with GPT-4 class models in a sandbox. Quality was good. But we can’t go to prod with that right now because of internal approvals and data residency concerns. We also tried some open models with vLLM on a single GPU box. It kind of works but performance and ops have been painful.

[05:27] Colin O'Donnell: Which open models?

[05:28] Tom Reynolds: Llama 3—uh, I think 70B? And Mixtral 8x7 at some point. Our eval is not super consistent yet.

[05:37] Fatima Noor: For this use case, the tradeoff tends to be: bigger model gives you better instruction following and fewer JSON breaks, but you pay in latency and cost. A common pattern is primary 70B class and a smaller fallback for overflow or less critical routes.

[05:53] Maya Patel: When you say fallback, do you mean a different model in the same environment, or calling out to a public endpoint as backup? Because the latter is a non-starter.

[06:02] Colin O'Donnell: Same environment. In Private we can set routing rules: if the primary is saturated or errors, you can fall back to a compatible smaller model that’s deployed alongside it.

[06:13] Tom Reynolds: That’s good. Our platform people will ask what happens under load. We can’t just fail everything.

[06:20] Hannah Schmitt: Right, graceful degradation.

[06:22] Colin O'Donnell: A question for you: are there multiple “routes” in the app? Like summary route vs compliance scan route.

[06:28] Tom Reynolds: Yes. Summary/chat route is interactive. Compliance scan is asynchronous. We could tolerate lower quality on scan as long as false negatives are low. Actually, sorry, that sounds contradictory.

[06:41] Fatima Noor: It’s common: for compliance you often want higher recall. That can be achieved with prompt patterns and maybe a different model tuned for classification. But for POC, we can keep it simple: one model plus guardrails.

[06:56] Elena Garcia: We also need audit logs on who asked what and what model answered. Not the whole content necessarily, but metadata.

[07:04] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. In Private you can export audit logs. We should align on what fields: request ID, timestamp, model version, route name, user ID (if you pass it), and result codes.

[07:18] Maya Patel: We’d like to send logs to Splunk. Is it JSON? Is it syslog?

[07:24] Colin O'Donnell: We can do JSON logs and ship via your existing logging pipeline. Typical is: Redwood components emit structured logs; you collect with your agent (Fluent Bit, whatever) and forward to Splunk or S3.

[07:36] Maya Patel: Okay.

[07:38] Hannah Schmitt: Elena, on retention, what’s the policy you need?

[07:43] Elena Garcia: The biggest question is: do you store prompts and outputs by default? We want “no” unless we explicitly turn it on for debugging. And even then, we need a short retention window.

[07:56] Fatima Noor: Understood. We can scope the POC as: no prompt/output persistence by Redwood beyond what’s required for serving, and you control your own application logs. For debugging, there are options, but we can keep them off.

[08:09] Elena Garcia: And encryption keys—customer-managed. We use AWS KMS.

[08:13] Colin O'Donnell: We can integrate with KMS for encryption at rest for volumes and any persisted artifacts. For the serving path, data is in memory; in transit is TLS. For POC we’ll document the boundaries.

[08:28] Maya Patel: On identity: we’ll probably want SSO eventually. For POC can we just use API keys and IP allowlisting?

[08:34] Fatima Noor: For a short eval, yes. But we should still design with the assumption you’ll map user identity into requests for auditability.

[08:44] Tom Reynolds: Our app will attach a user ID. We can include it in headers.

[08:48] Colin O'Donnell: Great.

[08:50] Hannah Schmitt: Switching gears: routing and fallback. Tom, can you describe your “must haves”?

[08:56] Tom Reynolds: Two things. One: if the model is unavailable, we’d rather degrade to a smaller model than error. But it must still produce valid JSON. Two: we might want “policy-based routing” later, like certain regions or certain data types stay in a specific cluster.

[09:14] Colin O'Donnell: For POC we can implement basic: route A uses model X, route B uses model X as well, and fallback to model Y on 5xx or queue depth. And everything stays in your VPC.

[09:28] Maya Patel: What about multi-region? We’re mostly US-East, but we have some EU clients.

[09:33] Hannah Schmitt: For this POC, do you need EU data residency day one?

[09:37] Elena Garcia: Not for the POC, but we will be asked if the platform supports EU isolation.

[09:44] Fatima Noor: We can answer at the architecture level: you can deploy Private in a given region, and you control data residency by where you deploy and route. But we should not over-commit to multi-region failover in the first two weeks.

[09:59] Maya Patel: Agree.

[10:02] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s map the POC timeline. You said two to three weeks. Is there a business deadline driving it?

[10:08] Tom Reynolds: We have an internal steering committee mid-Feb. If we can show a working integration and some benchmark results, that unlocks budget.

[10:19] Hannah Schmitt: Great. So what we propose:
Week 1: environment, connectivity, baseline performance tests with a few representative prompts.
Week 2: integrate into your app route, tune prompts/structured output, caching/batching as needed.
Week 3 (if needed): security review artifacts, sizing, and procurement readiness.

[10:40] Tom Reynolds: That matches.

[10:42] Maya Patel: Week 1 will be blocked on networking. I can get a network engineer assigned, but I need your checklist.

[10:49] Colin O'Donnell: I’ll send a checklist: VPC CIDRs, peering acceptance, security group ports, DNS resolution, and certificate assumptions. Also if you have outbound egress restrictions, we need to know.

[11:05] Maya Patel: We do. We have an allowlist.

[11:08] Colin O'Donnell: Okay, we’ll keep egress minimal.

[11:11] Hannah Schmitt: Tom, on evaluation harness—how are you planning to measure quality?

[11:16] Tom Reynolds: We have a small labeled set. Not huge. Mostly we’ll do human review and basic checks: JSON valid, citations refer to provided snippets, no prohibited claims. Eventually we’ll expand to a full eval suite.

[11:34] Fatima Noor: For POC, that’s fine. We can also add automatic checks for schema validity and citation format.

[11:42] Tom Reynolds: Yeah.

[11:44] Hannah Schmitt: Any “hard no’s” we should capture now? Things that would kill the POC.

[11:50] Elena Garcia: If we can’t get a clear answer on retention and if there’s any training on our data—hard no.

[11:57] Fatima Noor: For Private deployment, your data is not used to train Redwood models. We’ll put that in writing in the security addendum language.

[12:08] Elena Garcia: Good.

[12:10] Maya Patel: Also if we can’t get logs out. We need audit logs exportable.

[12:15] Colin O'Donnell: Understood.

[12:18] Hannah Schmitt: On models, Fatima, do you want to propose a starting set?

[12:22] Fatima Noor: Based on what you said—strict JSON, citations, interactive latency—I’d propose:
Option A: a 70B instruction model as primary for the interactive summary route.
Option B: a smaller 8B–13B instruction model as fallback and for batch compliance scan.
We can also test quantization profiles to hit latency targets. But we should be careful—quantization can impact instruction following.

[12:50] Tom Reynolds: Makes sense. We just need it to be consistent.

[12:55] Colin O'Donnell: Also, we can set max output tokens and stop sequences to reduce runaways. That helps latency.

[13:03] Tom Reynolds: Yep.

[13:04] Hannah Schmitt: And Redwood console—during the POC you’ll get visibility into token counts, latency by stage, error rates.

[13:12] Maya Patel: Will we have access? Or is it only your team?

[13:14] Hannah Schmitt: You’ll have access, with RBAC. For POC we can start with a couple admin users.

[13:22] Elena Garcia: RBAC is important but we can accept a minimal setup for POC.

[13:27] Colin O'Donnell: Totally.

[13:29] Tom Reynolds: Question: can you support tool calling? Like function calling?

[13:33] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. The API supports tool / function calling patterns. It depends on the model’s capabilities, but we can structure prompts accordingly. For POC, if you want, we can do a simpler “structured JSON” approach rather than full tool calling.

[13:49] Tom Reynolds: I think structured JSON is enough.

[13:52] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Let’s talk data flow boundaries explicitly so Elena can take notes. My understanding:
- Requests originate from your internal portal.
- Your retrieval system pulls snippets from your internal stores.
- You send the prompt + snippets to Redwood running inside your VPC.
- Redwood returns output.
- You log whatever you choose in your systems.
Is that correct?

[14:17] Maya Patel: Yes.

[14:19] Elena Garcia: And Redwood doesn’t retain prompts/outputs by default.

[14:22] Fatima Noor: Correct for how we’ll configure the POC.

[14:26] Elena Garcia: And any support access is controlled.

[14:30] Hannah Schmitt: Right. Support access would be break-glass and logged. For POC we can also set the expectation: no one from Redwood accesses your environment without explicit approval.

[14:43] Maya Patel: Good.

[14:45] Tom Reynolds: What about model updates? Like, if we pick a version, does it change underneath?

[14:50] Colin O'Donnell: For Private, you control upgrades. We can pin a model version for the POC so results are stable.

[14:58] Tom Reynolds: Great.

[15:00] Hannah Schmitt: Okay. I think we have enough to write up the plan. Let’s confirm owners and calendar items.

[15:07] Hannah Schmitt: Colin will send environment checklist by tomorrow. Tom and Maya, you’ll send sanitized prompts and workload stats—QPS, tokens, concurrency—by Friday. Elena, you’ll send the security questionnaire lite and required evidence list next week.

[15:25] Elena Garcia: Yes.

[15:26] Maya Patel: Yes.

[15:27] Tom Reynolds: Works.

[15:29] Hannah Schmitt: And we’ll schedule a 90-minute technical deep dive next week on routing/fallback and sizing. Colin, you’ll run that with Maya’s platform engineer.

[15:40] Colin O'Donnell: Yep.

[15:41] Maya Patel: I’ll bring whoever owns networking.

[15:43] Hannah Schmitt: Any last questions?

[15:46] Tom Reynolds: Just one. If we test and latency is too slow with the big model, what’s the knob? More GPUs, smaller model, or quantization?

[15:54] Colin O'Donnell: All three. In POC, easiest levers are: reduce max tokens, tune prompt to be concise, try a smaller model for certain routes, and apply safe quantization if quality holds. We’ll measure and iterate.

[16:09] Tom Reynolds: Great.

[16:10] Elena Garcia: And if we need documentation for auditors—what do we get?

[16:14] Fatima Noor: We can provide the security FAQ language and architecture diagram for Private/VPC, plus details on encryption, logging, and retention configuration. Some evidence may require NDA—Hannah can coordinate.

[16:30] Hannah Schmitt: Yep, I’ll follow up on NDA status and what we can share.

[16:35] Maya Patel: Cool.

[16:36] Hannah Schmitt: Thanks everyone. We’ll send a recap email with the POC plan and action items.

---
